periods.activity_title: Tiling and Jumping into the Greatest Common Factor

textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 30 and 50; (d) 28 and 42, find the longest jump size from 0 that lands on both numbers, and explain why it equals their HCF.
Find the common factors and HCF of 45 and 75. Using 45 = 3×3×5 and 75 = 3×5×5, the common subparts are 3, 5, 15, so common factors are 1, 3, 5, 15 and HCF = 15.

time_bands.activity: Pose the tiling scenario from the chapter opening: Sameeksha must tile a 12 ft × 16 ft room with the largest possible whole-number square tile. Students list the factors of 12 and 16 on their notebooks, circle the common ones, and identify the largest — establishing what a common factor is and why its greatest member matters.

Students play section 11.1 p.48 ("'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 30 and 50; (d) 28 and 42, find the longest jump size from 0 that lands on both numbers, and explain why it equals their HCF....") in pairs, recording jump sizes and articulating why the longest landing jump is the HCF.

Revisit primes and prime factorisation: students build the factorisation of 90, 105, and 30 using repeated division and verify that the prime factors are the same regardless of the starting divisor. The idea that every factor of a number is a 'subpart' of its prime factorisation is drawn out through 840 = 2×2×2×3×5×7, checking whether 28 is a factor.

Walk through Example 1, section 11.1 p.52 ("Find the common factors and HCF of 45 and 75. Using 45 = 3×3×5 and 75 = 3×5×5, the common subparts are 3, 5, 15, so common factors are 1, 3, 5, 15 and HCF = 15....") as a class, naming the rule: take each common prime the minimum number of times it appears across the numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often list factors by trial division and miss the link to prime factorisation — use the tiling context to make the 'subpart' language feel concrete before moving to notation. Watch for the error of taking the maximum, not the minimum, occurrence of a shared prime when identifying common subparts. Example 2, section 11.1 p.52, which handles 112 and 84, is a useful self-study follow-up for confident students.
materials: Squared paper or grid paper for tiling sketch

periods.activity_title: Prime Subparts in Action: Finding HCF by Factorisation

textbook_items_in_class.description: List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132; (d) 360 (24 factors); (e) 840 (32 factors), using prime factorisation.
Find the common factors and HCF of (a) 50, 60; (b) 140, 275; (c) 77, 725; (d) 370, 592; (e) 81, 243.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.1 p.54

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 11.1 p.54
homework.description: Given 72 = 6×12 and 144 = 8×18, decide whether one can conclude the two numbers have no common factor other than 1, and explain why not.

time_bands.activity: Open with Anshu's conjecture that larger numbers always have longer prime factorisations. Students check 121 = 11×11 against a two-digit number like 30 = 2×3×5 and articulate why the conjecture fails — practising the vocabulary of counterexample.

Students individually attempt Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.51 ("List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132; (d) 360 (24 factors); (e) 840 (32 factors), using prime factorisation...."), using prime factorisations to read off all factors systematically. Pairs compare lists for 225 to check for omissions.

In small groups, students work Figure it Out, section 11.1 p.53 ("Find the common factors and HCF of (a) 50, 60; (b) 140, 275; (c) 77, 725; (d) 370, 592; (e) 81, 243...."), focusing on parts (c) and (d) where the HCF is 1, connecting back to the rice-packing context of Lekhana.

Class works through Figure it Out Q1, section 11.1 p.54 ("Find the HCF of (a) 24, 180; (b) 42, 75, 24; (c) 240, 378; (d) 400, 2500; (e) 300, 800...."), with part (b) — three numbers — discussed together to confirm that the minimum-occurrence rule extends to more than two numbers.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that the HCF is the product of shared primes taken the minimum number of times each appears, this unit applies that rule across varied pairs. A frequent error is treating 'no common prime' as meaning HCF = 0 rather than HCF = 1 — emphasise that 1 divides every integer. Example 3, section 11.1 p.53, covering 96 and 275, supports that discussion.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for group results

periods.activity_title: Torans and Games: Meeting the Lowest Common Multiple

textbook_items_in_class.description: 'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 14 and 30; (d) 15 and 55, find the first number for which 'idli-vada' is called out, and decide whether the answer is always the LCM.
Find the LCM of 14 and 35. From 14 = 2×7 and 35 = 5×7, the LCM must contain 2×7 and 5×7 as subparts: the lowest is 2×5×7 = 70.

time_bands.activity: Pose the toran-making scenario: Anshu and Guna cut strips of 6 cm and 8 cm and need the shortest length that works for both without cutting. Students list the first several multiples of 6 and 8 on their notebooks, find the common ones, and identify the smallest — building the definition of LCM as the least of the common multiples.

Introduce the sweet-shop gajak problem (free every 7 days, visited every 10 days). Students compute multiples of 7 and multiples of 10 and locate the first common entry, then play section 11.2 p.56 ("'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 14 and 30; (d) 15 and 55, find the first number for which 'idli-vada' is called out, and decide whether the answer is always the LCM....") to check whether the first shared call-out is always the LCM.

Students examine why listing multiples becomes tedious for large numbers and explore the prime-factorisation method: comparing a number's factorisation with its multiple's shows the multiple's factorisation must contain the number's as a subpart. This structural observation — a common multiple must contain each number's prime subpart — is drawn out in discussion.

Walk through Example 6, section 11.2 p.56–57 ("Find the LCM of 14 and 35. From 14 = 2×7 and 35 = 5×7, the LCM must contain 2×7 and 5×7 as subparts: the lowest is 2×5×7 = 70....") step by step, naming the rule: take each prime the maximum number of times it occurs in either factorisation.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have just worked on HCF often confuse minimum (for HCF) with maximum (for LCM) — the toran and gajak contexts are worth returning to whenever the direction of the rule is uncertain. Watch for students listing only the LCM and skipping the justification that it is indeed the least common multiple. Example 7, section 11.2 p.57, which finds the LCM of 96 and 360, is a good self-study extension for confident students.
materials: Strips of paper (optional, for toran demonstration)

periods.activity_title: LCM by Prime Factorisation: Extended Practice

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the LCM of 96 and 360. From 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 360 = 2×2×2×3×3×5, take the maximum occurrences of each prime (five 2s, two 3s, one 5): LCM = 1440.

time_bands.activity: Review the maximum-occurrence rule by working through Example 7, section 11.2 p.57 ("Find the LCM of 96 and 360. From 96 = 2×2×2×2×2×3 and 360 = 2×2×2×3×3×5, take the maximum occurrences of each prime (five 2s, two 3s, one 5): LCM = 1440....") as a guided reconstruction — students supply each step and the teacher scribes.

Students individually attempt Figure it Out, section 11.2 p.58 ("Find the LCM of (a) 30, 72; (b) 36, 54; (c) 105, 195, 65; (d) 222, 370...."), writing out prime factorisations before identifying the maximum-occurrence primes. Part (c) — three numbers — prompts discussion of how the rule extends.

Pairs compare answers and resolve any discrepancies in parts (c) and (d) by returning to the prime subpart argument: does the proposed LCM contain each number's factorisation as a subpart? Students verify by division.

Whole-class consolidation: connect the toran context back to part (a) — 30 and 72 — by confirming that the computed LCM is indeed the shortest common length. Students state the maximum-occurrence rule in their own words and record it in their notebooks.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced the maximum-occurrence rule through examples, this unit cements it with multi-number cases. A common error is carrying only the maximum from the first factorisation and ignoring additional prime factors unique to the second number — the subpart-containment check in the second band catches this directly. For students who finish early, posing a word problem such as the gajak problem with three shops provides a natural three-number extension.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Generalising: When Is the HCF the Smaller Number?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers; (b) two consecutive odd numbers; (c) two even numbers; (d) two consecutive numbers; (e) two co-prime numbers.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given that the LCM of 3 and 24 is 24: (a) find more pairs where the LCM is one of the two numbers; (b) make a general statement about such numbers and describe them using algebra.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.59
textbook_items_in_class.description: Make and explain a general statement about the LCM of (a) two multiples of 3; (b) two consecutive even numbers; (c) two consecutive numbers; (d) two co-prime numbers.

time_bands.activity: Open with the observation from section 11.3: when 3 and 24 are considered, the LCM is 24 — one of the numbers itself. Students recall the prime-factorisation meaning of this (3's factorisation is a subpart of 24's) and articulate in their own words what kind of relationship between two numbers produces this, introducing the vocabulary 'generalisation' and 'general statement' as the chapter does.

In pairs, students work Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59 ("Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers; (b) two consecutive odd numbers; (c) two even numbers; (d) two consecutive numbers; (e) two co-prime numbers...."), testing several examples of each type, proposing a conjecture, and writing it as a general statement — using algebra where the chapter models it (e.g., n and 5n).

Groups continue with Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.59 ("Given that the LCM of 3 and 24 is 24: (a) find more pairs where the LCM is one of the two numbers; (b) make a general statement about such numbers and describe them using algebra....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.59 ("Make and explain a general statement about the LCM of (a) two multiples of 3; (b) two consecutive even numbers; (c) two consecutive numbers; (d) two co-prime numbers...."), gathering evidence and framing algebraic descriptions.

Class shares and critiques the general statements produced: students explain why each holds by returning to the prime subpart argument, and one pair's algebraic description of factor–multiple pairs (n and kn, with HCF = n) is displayed and discussed as a demonstration of how algebra expresses a pattern precisely.

periods.teacher_notes: The prime-factorisation understanding built for HCF and LCM is now the engine for reasoning about general patterns — naming that connection helps students see generalisation as an extension of what they already know, not a new topic. Watch for general statements that are correct in all tested cases but stated without a justification; prompt 'How do you know it always works?' to deepen the reasoning. The algebraic descriptions in Q2 and Q3 are the chapter's entry point into variable thinking and deserve unhurried discussion.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: The Combined Procedure and the HCF × LCM Property

textbook_items_in_class.description: For (a) 45, 105; (b) 275, 352; (c) 222, 370, explore whether the LCM is a factor of the product, find the multiplier that gives the product, and observe that it is the HCF (suggesting HCF × LCM = product).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the HCF and LCM (stating answers as prime factorisations) of (a) 3×3×5×7×7 and 12×7×11; (b) 45 and 36.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find two numbers whose HCF is 1 and LCM is 66.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the combined division procedure from section 11.3: both numbers are divided simultaneously by common primes until the quotients share no common factor. The HCF is the product of the divisors; the LCM is the divisors times the final quotients. Demonstrate with 45 and 105 on the board, then show Guna's shortcut of dividing by a larger composite common factor in one step.

Students work section 11.3 p.62 ("For (a) 45, 105; (b) 275, 352; (c) 222, 370, explore whether the LCM is a factor of the product, find the multiplier that gives the product, and observe that it is the HCF (suggesting HCF × LCM = product)....") and examine in each case how HCF × LCM compares to the product of the two numbers, recording the pattern and using prime-factor reasoning to explain why the common primes go into the HCF while the non-common ones go into the LCM.

Students work Figure it Out Q3, section 11.3 p.63 ("Find the HCF and LCM (stating answers as prime factorisations) of (a) 3×3×5×7×7 and 12×7×11; (b) 45 and 36...."), expressing both HCF and LCM as prime factorisations and then verifying HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers for each pair.

Figure it Out Q4, section 11.3 p.63 ("Find two numbers whose HCF is 1 and LCM is 66....") turns the property around: students use HCF × LCM = product to constrain the search, list factor pairs of 66, and identify those that are co-prime. The question of whether HCF × LCM = product extends to three numbers is posed as an open investigation.

periods.teacher_notes: The generalisation that HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers follows from the prime-subpart understanding students have built — stress that the common primes contribute once to the HCF (minimum) and once to the LCM (maximum), together accounting for the full product. A frequent error is applying HCF × LCM = product to three numbers without checking; the closing open question is designed to surface this. Figure it Out Q2, section 11.3 p.63, on factor-and-multiple checks, is a useful parallel self-study item.

textbook_segments.title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!

periods.activity_title: Puzzles, Folklore, and Fractions: HCF and LCM at Work

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 11.3 p.63
textbook_items_in_class.description: Karnataka folklore problem: a cowherd's cows pass in equal groups through crossings of 3, 5, and 7 gates; with fewer than 200 cows, find how many cows he had.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: A box is 12 cm × 18 cm × 36 cm; decide which cubes of side (a) 9 cm; (b) 6 cm; (c) 4 cm; (d) 3 cm; (e) 2 cm can be packed without gaps.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q13, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mahaviracharya's problem (850 CE): add 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63, and 1/21, and find an efficient way to compute the sum (using the LCM of the denominators).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 11.3 p.64
textbook_items_in_class.description: In 'Fire in the Mountain', no one is out for 6 or 9 but some are out for 10; choose how many children could have been playing initially from (a) 72; (b) 90; (c) 45; (d) 3; (e) 36; (f) None of these.

time_bands.activity: Students tackle Figure it Out Q5, section 11.3 p.63 ("Karnataka folklore problem: a cowherd's cows pass in equal groups through crossings of 3, 5, and 7 gates; with fewer than 200 cows, find how many cows he had....") individually: the number must be divisible by 3, 5, and 7, so the LCM of 3, 5, 7 gives the smallest candidate; checking the constraint of fewer than 200 confirms the answer.

In pairs, students work Figure it Out Q6, section 11.3 p.64 ("A box is 12 cm × 18 cm × 36 cm; decide which cubes of side (a) 9 cm; (b) 6 cm; (c) 4 cm; (d) 3 cm; (e) 2 cm can be packed without gaps...."), reasoning that a cube's side must divide all three dimensions of the box — equivalently, the cube's side must be a common factor of 12, 18, and 36.

Students work Figure it Out Q13, section 11.3 p.64 ("Mahaviracharya's problem (850 CE): add 8/15, 1/20, 7/36, 11/63, and 1/21, and find an efficient way to compute the sum (using the LCM of the denominators)...."), first computing the LCM of 15, 20, 36, 63, and 21 using prime factorisation, then converting each fraction to the common denominator and summing. The historical context of Mahaviracharya (850 CE) is noted.

Whole-class discussion of Figure it Out Q9, section 11.3 p.64 ("In 'Fire in the Mountain', no one is out for 6 or 9 but some are out for 10; choose how many children could have been playing initially...."), requiring students to identify a number that is not divisible by 6 or 9 but is divisible by 10 — a divisibility and LCM puzzle that brings the chapter's ideas together in a game context.

periods.teacher_notes: The cube-packing problem hinges on recognising that a divisor of all three dimensions must be a common factor — connecting the HCF idea back to a three-number real context. Watch for students confusing 'divisible by 3, 5, and 7' with 'divisible by 3+5+7' in the cowherd problem; the LCM-as-product reasoning applies here only because 3, 5, and 7 are pairwise co-prime. Mahaviracharya's fraction sum rewards careful prime factorisation of five denominators and provides a historically grounded close to the chapter.

items.prompt: A number's prime factorisation is 2 × 2 × 3 × 5. Which of the following is a factor of this number?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 15. Since 15 = 3 × 5, it is a subpart of 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 and is therefore a factor.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Check whether each option's prime factorisation appears as a subpart of the given prime factorisation.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be guessing or confusing factors with multiples, as 7 does not appear in the factorisation at all.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student likely thinks that any product of repeated factors present in the factorisation qualifies; 8 = 2×2×2 requires three 2s, but only two are available.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may believe that any prime appearing in the factorisation can be squared freely; 9 = 3×3 requires two 3s, but only one is present.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write the factorisation 2×2×3×5 on paper and try to form each option from those digits.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to list all twelve factors of 60 using only the prime factorisation, without trial division.

exercise.description: 'Jump Jackpot' game: for treasures on (a) 14 and 30; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 30 and 50; (d) 28 and 42, find the longest jump size from 0 that lands on both numbers, and explain why it equals their HCF.

items.prompt: Priya calls out multiples of 4 and Raju calls out multiples of 6. What is the smallest number they both call out at the same time?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, since 4 = 2×2 and 6 = 2×3, giving LCM = 2×2×3 = 12.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the prime-factorisation LCM rule: take each prime the maximum number of times it occurs in either factorisation.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student likely listed common multiples correctly but chose the second rather than the first (least) one.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student may be confusing LCM with HCF, as 2 is the HCF of 4 and 6.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may think the LCM of two numbers is always one of those numbers, picking the smaller.

inclusivity.support: Let the student write out the first ten multiples of 4 and the first ten multiples of 6 and circle shared values.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to state, as a general rule, when the LCM of two numbers equals their product, and give an example.

exercise.description: 'Idli-Vada' game: for the number pairs (a) 4 and 6; (b) 7 and 11; (c) 14 and 30; (d) 15 and 55, find the first number for which 'idli-vada' is called out, and decide whether the answer is always the LCM.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: Two consecutive numbers are chosen, such as 8 and 9. Make a general statement about the HCF of any two consecutive numbers, and explain why it must always be true using the idea of prime factorisations or common factors.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The HCF of any two consecutive numbers is always 1. Any factor of n also divides n+1 only if it divides their difference, which is 1; so no number greater than 1 can divide both. Equivalently, consecutive numbers share no prime factor.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the reasoning that a common factor of n and n+1 must divide their difference (n+1) − n = 1, so it can only be 1.

inclusivity.support: Invite the student to try three pairs of consecutive numbers, list each number's factors, and share observations before writing the general statement.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to adapt the argument for two consecutive even numbers and decide whether the HCF is always 2, always greater than 2, or depends on the numbers.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 11.3 p.59
exercise.description: Make and explain a general statement about the HCF of (a) two consecutive even numbers; (b) two consecutive odd numbers; (c) two even numbers; (d) two consecutive numbers; (e) two co-prime numbers.

items.prompt: A school hall floor measures 48 m × 36 m. The principal wants to tile it with the largest possible identical square tiles that fit exactly without cutting. Find the side length of each tile.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 12 m. Prime factorisations: 48 = 2×2×2×2×3 and 36 = 2×2×3×3. Common primes taken the minimum number of times: 2×2×3 = 12. So the largest square tile has a side of 12 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the HCF of 48 and 36 using prime factorisation: take each common prime the minimum number of times it appears in either factorisation.

inclusivity.support: Offer a number-line or factor-tree sketch on which the student marks the prime factors of 48 and 36 before identifying the shared ones.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find how many such tiles are needed to cover the whole floor, and verify the answer by computing 48 × 36 ÷ 12².

exercise.description: List all the factors of (a) 90; (b) 105; (c) 132; (d) 360 (24 factors); (e) 840 (32 factors), using prime factorisation.

items.prompt: Three bells ring at intervals of 12 minutes, 18 minutes, and 30 minutes. They all ring together at noon. After how many minutes will they next all ring together?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 180 minutes. Prime factorisations: 12 = 2×2×3, 18 = 2×3×3, 30 = 2×3×5. Taking each prime the maximum number of times: 2×2×3×3×5 = 180. The bells next ring together after 180 minutes.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the LCM of 12, 18, and 30 using prime factorisation: take each prime the maximum number of times it occurs in any one of the three factorisations.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first find the LCM of any two bells, then find the LCM of that result with the third bell's interval.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find the LCM of 12, 18, and 30 a second way — by using the property HCF × LCM = product applied stepwise — and verify that both methods agree.

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: The HCF of two numbers is 14 and their LCM is 168. One of the two numbers is 56. Find the other number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 42. Using HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers: 14 × 168 = 2352. The other number = 2352 ÷ 56 = 42. Check: 56 = 2×2×2×7, 42 = 2×3×7; HCF = 2×7 = 14 ✓, LCM = 2×2×2×3×7 = 168 ✓.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers, then divide by the known number.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student of the property HCF × LCM = product, and ask them to compute 14 × 168 first before dividing.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the answer by finding the prime factorisations of both numbers and confirming that HCF and LCM read off correctly from them.

exercise.description: For (a) 45, 105; (b) 275, 352; (c) 222, 370, explore whether the LCM is a factor of the product, find the multiplier that gives the product, and observe that it is the HCF (suggesting HCF × LCM = product).

items.section_title: Patterns, Properties, and a Pretty Procedure!
items.prompt: A cowherd has fewer than 100 cows. When he drives them through a gate that fits exactly 4 cows abreast, none are left over. When the gate fits exactly 6 cows abreast, none are left over. When the gate fits exactly 9 cows abreast, none are left over. How many cows does he have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 36. The number of cows must be divisible by 4, 6, and 9. Prime factorisations: 4 = 2×2, 6 = 2×3, 9 = 3×3. LCM = 2×2×3×3 = 36. Since 36 < 100 and the next multiple is 72, both 36 and 72 are valid; the smallest is 36. (If the problem requires a unique answer less than 100, both 36 and 72 satisfy it; the least is 36.)
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the LCM of 4, 6, and 9; list its multiples below 100 to identify all possible answers.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student start by finding the LCM of just 4 and 6, then find the LCM of that result with 9.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to change one gate size to 5 and find how many cows (fewer than 200) satisfy all three conditions in that new version.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 11.3 p.63
exercise.description: Karnataka folklore problem: a cowherd's cows pass in equal groups through crossings of 3, 5, and 7 gates; with fewer than 200 cows, find how many cows he had.
